_what_this_is: EVERY state the two update surfaces can be in, and what each one must say.
One table, both readers: the briefing line (framework/frontdoor/run_briefing,
_update_notice + _update_refusal_line, pytest) and the home card
(cabinet/dashboard/src/lib/updates, updateHeadline + refusalToShow, vitest).
Each reader is driven on the SAME bytes -- `state` is written verbatim as
.updates/state.json, and the card fixture is derived from these fields
exactly as `cabinet-update.sh status --json` derives its report.
WHY AN EXHAUSTIVE TABLE AND NOT MORE ARMS. Three review rounds each found one
more adjacent state in these same two readers: a refusal that outlived the
bundle it was about (round 1), a refusal that spoke over a running apply
(round 2), a refusal that outlived the apply that overtook it (round 3).
Every arm written for each of them was aimed at the state that already
worked. Hand-written arms cannot close that class, because the defect is
always in the state nobody thought to write an arm for. A product does not
have to be thought of.
THE AXES (5 x 3 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 240 rows, the whole product, nothing skipped):
phase          idle | refused | applying | applied | rolled_back
waiting        none | same (the bundle the refusal is about) | other
refusal        none | locked-paths | busy | digest-mismatch
ledger_error   absent | set (A5.16: the ledger FAILED, not a version behind)
event_fallback false | true (a record held for a ledger one version behind)
`waiting` folds presence and sha identity into one 3-valued axis; a refusal is
always ABOUT the `refused` sha, so `same`/`other` is what scopes it. Rows that
cannot arise from the updater (phase `idle` carrying a refusal, phase `refused`
carrying none) are KEPT and pinned: a state file can be truncated or
hand-edited, and what a reader does at the degenerate end is exactly what
three rounds of arms never asked.
THE RULES, from the contract (A5.13, A5.15, A5.16) and not from either
implementation. `refusal_speaks` is the sub-surface -- refusalToShow non-null
on the card, a non-empty _update_refusal_line on the briefing -- and it is the
same on BOTH surfaces on every row, because it is one property of one record:
1. No refusal on record: it never speaks.
2. An apply IN FLIGHT outranks it. `applying` is the live state; a refusal
recorded before the retry that is running now is a note about a request.
3. Nothing waiting: it speaks only while it is still the LAST THING THAT
HAPPENED, i.e. phase `refused`. An apply or a rollback since has
overtaken it, and `last_refusal` is carried through every write for ever,
so without this rule one refusal silences the applied and rolled-back
sentences on both surfaces for the life of the install.
4. Something waiting: it speaks only if it is a verdict ON THOSE BYTES --
the same sha, and a reason about the bundle rather than about timing
(`busy` means another updater held the lock).
THE HEADLINE KINDS: ready | refused | applying | applied | rolled_back |
fault | quiet. The two surfaces rank them the same except for one deliberate
difference of SHAPE, which is written per surface here rather than skipped:
the briefing has ONE line and spends it on a ledger fault above everything
but a refusal (A5.16 -- a full disk announced as a version number is a fault
nobody goes back to look at), while the card has room to show the fault as a
sub-line beside whatever its headline says. That is the only axis on which
`briefing` and `card` may differ; the wording differs everywhere, which is why
what is asserted is the kind.
A FAULT IS NEVER HEADLINE-LESS. The card renders at all only when its
headline is non-null, so `fault` is the card's LAST arm: it takes the
headline only where nothing else has one, which is the only way `named on
every surface` can be true of a surface that can decline to appear.
A kind flipped here reds BOTH suites. A row whose code disagrees with this
table is a defect in the code -- this table is derived from the contract, and
the code is what has been wrong three times.
